How do I actually file my claim, and what does it cost?

Where things stand

You can file in the territorial division where the problem happened or a defendant lives or does business, or where the court sits nearest to where a defendant lives or does business. Under the Limitations Act, 2002, a claim is discovered on the earlier of two days. One is the day you first knew certain facts; the other is the first day a reasonable person with your abilities and in your circumstances ought to have known them. There are four facts. First, that the loss happened. Second, that an act or omission caused it or helped cause it. Third, whose act it was. Fourth, that a court case is a fitting way to try to remedy it, given the kind of loss. You are presumed to have known them on the day of the act or omission, unless shown otherwise.

What to do next

If your claim is based on a document, attach a copy to each copy of the claim; if it is unavailable, the claim must say why. On paper, you file your Plaintiff's Claim (Form 7A) in person or by mail at the court office, with copies for you and each defendant. Online, you do not need extra copies; Toronto uses the Ontario Courts Public Portal, and other regions use the Small Claims Court Submissions Online portal. The fee is $108, or $228 if you filed 10 or more claims at that office this calendar year. If you cannot afford the fees, you may ask for a fee waiver; online, you say so when you submit.

Your deadline

The general deadline to start a court case. You have 2 years after the day the claim was discovered. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 2 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This applies unless the Limitations Act, 2002 provides otherwise. For example, a claim based on a sexual assault has no limitation period.

A deadline in an Ontario statute is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, unless the statute shows otherwise. When a period is described as starting after a day, that day is not counted (s. 89 (5)). If the last day is a Sunday or a holiday, the deadline moves to the next day that is not a holiday (s. 89 (1)). Saturday is not a holiday under that Act, so a Saturday does not by itself move the deadline. Some deadlines are for doing something at a place, such as filing at an office. If that place is not open during its regular hours on the last day, the deadline moves to the next day it is open during its regular hours (s. 89 (2)).

What happens after

Court staff review online filings within 3 business days. You cannot file online to meet a deadline that is 3 business days away or less. The clerk then issues the claim and gives it a court file number. Online, you get an email once the claim is issued. On paper, the clerk returns stamped copies for you to serve on each defendant.

Read more of the decision

[89] The first element of civil fraud is a false representation by the defendant. The Court of Appeal agreed with the motion judge that “[u]nquestionably, the Mauldin group was induced to invest with Hryniak because of what Hryniak said to Fred Mauldin” at the meeting of June 19, 2001 (at para. 158), and this was not disputed in the appellant’s factum. [90] The motion judge found the requisite knowledge or recklessness as to the falsehood of the representation, the second element of civil fraud, based on Hryniak’s lack of effort to ensure that the funds would be properly invested and failure to verify that the eventual end-point of the funds, New Savings Bank, was secure. The motion judge also rejected the defence that the funds were stolen, noting Hryniak’s feeble efforts to recover the funds, waiting some 15 months to report the apparent theft of US$10.2 million. [91] The motion judge also found an intention on the part of Hryniak that the Mauldin Group would act on his false representations, the third requirement of civil fraud. Hryniak secured a US$76,000 loan for Fred Mauldin and conducted a “test trade”, actions which, in the motion judge’s view, were “undertaken . . . for the purpose of dissuading the Mauldin group from demanding the return of its investment” (para. 113). Moreover, the motion judge detailed Hryniak’s central role in the web of deception that caused the Mauldin Group to invest its funds and that dissuaded them from seeking their return for some time after they had been stolen.

How do I actually file my claim, and what does it cost?

Where things stand

You can file in the territorial division where the problem happened or a defendant lives or does business, or where the court sits nearest to where a defendant lives or does business. Under the Limitations Act, 2002, a claim is discovered on the earlier of two days. One is the day you first knew certain facts; the other is the first day a reasonable person with your abilities and in your circumstances ought to have known them. There are four facts. First, that the loss happened. Second, that an act or omission caused it or helped cause it. Third, whose act it was. Fourth, that a court case is a fitting way to try to remedy it, given the kind of loss. You are presumed to have known them on the day of the act or omission, unless shown otherwise.

What to do next

If your claim is based on a document, attach a copy to each copy of the claim; if it is unavailable, the claim must say why. On paper, you file your Plaintiff's Claim (Form 7A) in person or by mail at the court office, with copies for you and each defendant. Online, you do not need extra copies; Toronto uses the Ontario Courts Public Portal, and other regions use the Small Claims Court Submissions Online portal. The fee is $108, or $228 if you filed 10 or more claims at that office this calendar year. If you cannot afford the fees, you may ask for a fee waiver; online, you say so when you submit.

Your deadline

The general deadline to start a court case. You have 2 years after the day the claim was discovered. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 2 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This applies unless the Limitations Act, 2002 provides otherwise. For example, a claim based on a sexual assault has no limitation period.

A deadline in an Ontario statute is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, unless the statute shows otherwise. When a period is described as starting after a day, that day is not counted (s. 89 (5)). If the last day is a Sunday or a holiday, the deadline moves to the next day that is not a holiday (s. 89 (1)). Saturday is not a holiday under that Act, so a Saturday does not by itself move the deadline. Some deadlines are for doing something at a place, such as filing at an office. If that place is not open during its regular hours on the last day, the deadline moves to the next day it is open during its regular hours (s. 89 (2)).

What happens after

Court staff review online filings within 3 business days. You cannot file online to meet a deadline that is 3 business days away or less. The clerk then issues the claim and gives it a court file number. Online, you get an email once the claim is issued. On paper, the clerk returns stamped copies for you to serve on each defendant.

How do I actually file my claim, and what does it cost?

Where things stand

You can file in the territorial division where the problem happened or a defendant lives or does business, or where the court sits nearest to where a defendant lives or does business. Under the Limitations Act, 2002, a claim is discovered on the earlier of two days. One is the day you first knew certain facts; the other is the first day a reasonable person with your abilities and in your circumstances ought to have known them. There are four facts. First, that the loss happened. Second, that an act or omission caused it or helped cause it. Third, whose act it was. Fourth, that a court case is a fitting way to try to remedy it, given the kind of loss. You are presumed to have known them on the day of the act or omission, unless shown otherwise.

What to do next

If your claim is based on a document, attach a copy to each copy of the claim; if it is unavailable, the claim must say why. On paper, you file your Plaintiff's Claim (Form 7A) in person or by mail at the court office, with copies for you and each defendant. Online, you do not need extra copies; Toronto uses the Ontario Courts Public Portal, and other regions use the Small Claims Court Submissions Online portal. The fee is $108, or $228 if you filed 10 or more claims at that office this calendar year. If you cannot afford the fees, you may ask for a fee waiver; online, you say so when you submit.

Your deadline

The general deadline to start a court case. You have 2 years after the day the claim was discovered. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 2 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This applies unless the Limitations Act, 2002 provides otherwise. For example, a claim based on a sexual assault has no limitation period.

A deadline in an Ontario statute is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, unless the statute shows otherwise. When a period is described as starting after a day, that day is not counted (s. 89 (5)). If the last day is a Sunday or a holiday, the deadline moves to the next day that is not a holiday (s. 89 (1)). Saturday is not a holiday under that Act, so a Saturday does not by itself move the deadline. Some deadlines are for doing something at a place, such as filing at an office. If that place is not open during its regular hours on the last day, the deadline moves to the next day it is open during its regular hours (s. 89 (2)).

What happens after

Court staff review online filings within 3 business days. You cannot file online to meet a deadline that is 3 business days away or less. The clerk then issues the claim and gives it a court file number. Online, you get an email once the claim is issued. On paper, the clerk returns stamped copies for you to serve on each defendant.

[90] The motion judge found the requisite knowledge or recklessness as to the falsehood of the representation, the second element of civil fraud, based on Hryniak’s lack of effort to ensure that the funds would be properly invested and failure to verify that the eventual end-point of the funds, New Savings Bank, was secure. The motion judge also rejected the defence that the funds were stolen, noting Hryniak’s feeble efforts to recover the funds, waiting some 15 months to report the apparent theft of US$10.2 million. [91] The motion judge also found an intention on the part of Hryniak that the Mauldin Group would act on his false representations, the third requirement of civil fraud. Hryniak secured a US$76,000 loan for Fred Mauldin and conducted a “test trade”, actions which, in the motion judge’s view, were “undertaken . . . for the purpose of dissuading the Mauldin group from demanding the return of its investment” (para. 113). Moreover, the motion judge detailed Hryniak’s central role in the web of deception that caused the Mauldin Group to invest its funds and that dissuaded them from seeking their return for some time after they had been stolen.

How do I actually file my claim, and what does it cost?

Where things stand

You can file in the territorial division where the problem happened or a defendant lives or does business, or where the court sits nearest to where a defendant lives or does business. Under the Limitations Act, 2002, a claim is discovered on the earlier of two days. One is the day you first knew certain facts; the other is the first day a reasonable person with your abilities and in your circumstances ought to have known them. There are four facts. First, that the loss happened. Second, that an act or omission caused it or helped cause it. Third, whose act it was. Fourth, that a court case is a fitting way to try to remedy it, given the kind of loss. You are presumed to have known them on the day of the act or omission, unless shown otherwise.

What to do next

If your claim is based on a document, attach a copy to each copy of the claim; if it is unavailable, the claim must say why. On paper, you file your Plaintiff's Claim (Form 7A) in person or by mail at the court office, with copies for you and each defendant. Online, you do not need extra copies; Toronto uses the Ontario Courts Public Portal, and other regions use the Small Claims Court Submissions Online portal. The fee is $108, or $228 if you filed 10 or more claims at that office this calendar year. If you cannot afford the fees, you may ask for a fee waiver; online, you say so when you submit.

Your deadline

The general deadline to start a court case. You have 2 years after the day the claim was discovered. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 2 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This applies unless the Limitations Act, 2002 provides otherwise. For example, a claim based on a sexual assault has no limitation period.

A deadline in an Ontario statute is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, unless the statute shows otherwise. When a period is described as starting after a day, that day is not counted (s. 89 (5)). If the last day is a Sunday or a holiday, the deadline moves to the next day that is not a holiday (s. 89 (1)). Saturday is not a holiday under that Act, so a Saturday does not by itself move the deadline. Some deadlines are for doing something at a place, such as filing at an office. If that place is not open during its regular hours on the last day, the deadline moves to the next day it is open during its regular hours (s. 89 (2)).

What happens after

Court staff review online filings within 3 business days. You cannot file online to meet a deadline that is 3 business days away or less. The clerk then issues the claim and gives it a court file number. Online, you get an email once the claim is issued. On paper, the clerk returns stamped copies for you to serve on each defendant.

Hryniak v. Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7, paras. 89-91

“The first element of civil fraud is a false representation by the defendant.”

A court decision: what the judges said in an earlier case. It has not been checked for later decisions that may have changed it.

Read more of the decision

[89] The first element of civil fraud is a false representation by the defendant. The Court of Appeal agreed with the motion judge that “[u]nquestionably, the Mauldin group was induced to invest with Hryniak because of what Hryniak said to Fred Mauldin” at the meeting of June 19, 2001 (at para. 158), and this was not disputed in the appellant’s factum. [90] The motion judge found the requisite knowledge or recklessness as to the falsehood of the representation, the second element of civil fraud, based on Hryniak’s lack of effort to ensure that the funds would be properly invested and failure to verify that the eventual end-point of the funds, New Savings Bank, was secure. The motion judge also rejected the defence that the funds were stolen, noting Hryniak’s feeble efforts to recover the funds, waiting some 15 months to report the apparent theft of US$10.2 million. [91] The motion judge also found an intention on the part of Hryniak that the Mauldin Group would act on his false representations, the third requirement of civil fraud. Hryniak secured a US$76,000 loan for Fred Mauldin and conducted a “test trade”, actions which, in the motion judge’s view, were “undertaken . . . for the purpose of dissuading the Mauldin group from demanding the return of its investment” (para. 113). Moreover, the motion judge detailed Hryniak’s central role in the web of deception that caused the Mauldin Group to invest its funds and that dissuaded them from seeking their return for some time after they had been stolen.

Checklist: Making a claim Prepare your claim carefully. It will make it easier for all parties to understand who is making the claim and exactly what is being claimed. Fill out a Plaintiff's Claim [Form 7A] or Defendant's Claim [Form 10A] . Attach an Additional Parties [Form 1A] if there is more than one plaintiff or defendant, or the defendant is known by more than one name and there is insufficient space on the claim form. Be sure to check the "additional parties" box on the claim form. File both the original claim and supporting documents, and a copy for yourself and each defendant, in person or by mail with the court, or file the claim and supporting documents online using the Small Claims Court Submissions Online portal. If you filed in person or by mail, the clerk will stamp the documents, keep the original, and return the copies to you. If you filed online, the court will e-mail you confirming your documents have been e-filed or e-issued. Make sure you print from the Ministry's website, or pick up from the court office, the "Guide to Serving Documents" and enough copies of the Affidavit of Service [Form 8A] to allow you to complete the affidavits required in step 8. If you are filing a plaintiff's claim, make sure you are filing your claim in the proper territorial jurisdiction. If you are filing a defendant's claim, file your claim with the court office where the plaintiff's claim was filed. Remember it must be filed within 20 days after the defence is filed unless the court orders otherwise. Pay the filing fee.

What the rules say about starting a Small Claims action

General information from the Rules of the Small Claims Court. You fill in and file the form yourself; the Plaintiff's Claim section below walks through what it asks for.

Filing the Plaintiff's Claim (Form 7A). An action is started by filing a Plaintiff's Claim (Form 7A) with the court clerk, with a copy for each defendant. If it is filed electronically, the extra copies are not needed. (r. 7.01(1), (1.1))
The clerk issues the claim. When the clerk receives the claim, the clerk issues it by dating, signing and sealing it and giving it a court file number. (r. 7.02(1))
Serving the claim. The claim has to be served on the defendant, personally or by an alternative to personal service the rules allow, within six months after it is issued. The court can extend that time, before or after the six months. (r. 8.01(1), (2))
The defendant's response. A defendant who wants to dispute the claim has 20 days after being served to serve a Defence (Form 9A) on every other party and file it, with proof of service, with the clerk. (r. 9.01)

Under s. 4 of the Limitations Act, 2002, unless the Act provides otherwise, a proceeding cannot be started after the second anniversary of the day the claim was discovered. Read more
Section 5(1) says when a claim is discovered: the earlier of the day the person first knew that the injury, loss or damage had occurred, that it was caused or contributed to by an act or omission, that the act or omission was that of the person the claim is against, and that, having regard to the nature of the injury, loss or damage, a proceeding would be an appropriate means to seek to remedy it -- and the day a reasonable person with their abilities and in their circumstances first ought to have known those things. Under s. 5(2), a person with a claim is presumed to have known of those matters on the day the act or omission the claim is based on took place, unless the contrary is proved.
